source_message.text:
Most importantly, I want the opening V to become recognizable enough over time to stand independently as a long-term brand asset. It should never require a separate icon or monogram; the wordmark itself should become the identity. This project is ultimately not about designing a beautiful font. The objective is a proprietary wordmark that feels inevitable, as though VEILLVÉ could never have been written another way.

That goal depends on recognizing that the brand signature is no longer just the accent over the É. It is the complete **V language**. The larger opening V should serve as the hero of the wordmark, while both the smaller closing V and the É accent should grow from that opening form’s geometry. Across these three elements, the angles, proportions, and material language should be identical. Even if every other letter were covered and only the two Vs and the accent remained visible, the result should still feel unmistakably like VEILLVÉ.

Everything else in the lettering needs to support the V rather than compete for attention. Our strongest direction treated those remaining letters as quiet, sculptural, intentional architectural objects instead of conventional typography. The kerning should be adjusted until the wordmark reads as one continuous mark rather than "VEI LL VÉ." The Ls should gain a more structural quality through taller architectural proportions and subtle custom geometry, without relying on decorative serifs. Likewise, the É accent should become a true brand signature rather than punctuation by being slightly shorter, thicker, and more closely integrated with the V geometry.

Restrained internal reveal lines or dimensional details can also be tested to add depth without becoming ornamental. The mark should feel capable of existing as a beautifully fabricated brass or stone sign whose details naturally catch the light. At the same time, we learned that pushing the architectural quality too far made the logo feel severe. It still needs to be timeless and sculptural while communicating warmth, vitality, and aspiration. That warmth should come through champagne metal, light, subtle illumination, and depth—not through softer or more decorative typography.

After months of refining this direction, these are the additional thoughts that best clarify where I believe the identity should go. Please challenge the typography where needed while preserving this design language; refining the wordmark’s existing DNA matters more to me than introducing an entirely unrelated idea.
